title: Old Elam
subtitle: 3,200–1,500 BC · Awan, Shimashki and the Sukkalmah

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Awan, the Shimashki kings, and the Sukkalmah's shared kingship

entries.label: The Awan Dynasty and the Treaty with Akkad
entries.hint: Known chiefly from the Sumerian King List and a treaty with Naram-Sin of Akkad, the Awan kings ruled a Susa-centred Elamite state contemporary with Sargon's Akkadian empire — one of the earliest Elamite dynasties documented well enough to be dated and sequenced, even where most individual kings remain little more than names.
entries.note: Sumerian King List, Awan dynasty section; the Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre.

entries.label: Puzur-Inshushinak — the Conqueror King
entries.hint: The last and most powerful Awan king, Puzur-Inshushinak briefly conquered large parts of southern Mesopotamia during Akkad's collapse, leaving royal inscriptions in both Akkadian and the newly invented Linear Elamite script — before Ur-Nammu of the rising Third Dynasty of Ur reversed his conquests entirely.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

entries.label: The Shimashki Dynasty and the Sack of Ur
entries.hint: Succeeding Awan, the Shimashki kings are known largely through their culminating achievement: Kindattu's army sacked Ur in 2004 BC, capturing King Ibbi-Sin and ending the Third Dynasty of Ur — the single most consequential Elamite military success against Mesopotamia in the entire Bronze Age.
entries.note: The Lament for Ur (Sumerian literary text); Elamite king list traditions preserved in later Mesopotamian sources.

entries.label: The Sukkalmah — Shared Kingship
entries.hint: The long Sukkalmah (or Epartid) period governed Elam through a distinctive triarchic system — a sukkalmah ('grand regent') at Susa, a sukkal of Elam and Shimashki, and a sukkal of Susa itself, typically an uncle, nephew and brother — an institutionalised power-sharing arrangement with no real parallel in contemporary Mesopotamian kingship.
entries.note: Sukkalmah-period administrative and legal tablets from Susa; Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The treaty with Akkad, the sack of Ur, and the wars with Babylon

entries.label: The Naram-Sin Treaty Ends a War
entries.hint: The treaty between Naram-Sin of Akkad and an Elamite king, sworn by both the Mesopotamian and Elamite pantheons, formally ended a period of conflict between the two powers and bound the Elamite ruler as a subordinate ally — the occasion for the oldest surviving connected text written in the Elamite language.

entries.label: Puzur-Inshushinak's Mesopotamian Campaigns
entries.hint: Exploiting the Akkadian Empire's collapse, Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions claim conquests reaching well into southern Mesopotamia — a high-water mark of Elamite military reach that proved as short-lived as the Akkadian power vacuum that had made it possible.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, on his claimed conquests.

entries.label: Kindattu Sacks Ur
entries.hint: An Elamite army under Kindattu, joined by forces from Shimashki's allies, stormed Ur and carried King Ibbi-Sin into captivity in Elam — an event Sumerian scribes mourned for generations afterward in the 'Lament for the Destruction of Sumer and Ur,' ending the Third Dynasty of Ur and one of Mesopotamia's great imperial revivals.
entries.note: The Lament for Ur; Sumerian King List, on the end of the Ur III dynasty.

entries.label: Hammurabi Defeats an Elamite-Led Coalition
entries.hint: Hammurabi's own year-names record a decisive victory over an alliance including Elam, Assyria and other regional powers — a reversal of the earlier alliance in which an Elamite-backed coalition had helped Hammurabi's Babylon against Larsa, showing how quickly the era's shifting alignments could turn former allies into declared enemies.
entries.note: Hammurabi's year-name list, on the defeat of the Elamite coalition.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Triarchic succession and the dual Akkadian-Elamite administration

entries.label: Triarchic Succession
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-period succession passed kingship laterally — typically from brother to brother before descending to the next generation's eldest nephew — rather than directly from father to son, a deliberate system that kept power within a wide circle of the royal family and may have reduced (without eliminating) succession disputes common under strict primogeniture.
entries.note: Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History, on the succession pattern reconstructed from dated tablets.

entries.label: Dual Akkadian-Elamite Administration
entries.hint: Susa's administrative and legal tablets from this period were written in both Akkadian and Elamite, sometimes within the same archive, reflecting a genuinely bilingual bureaucratic culture at the crossroads of the Elamite highlands and the Mesopotamian lowland tradition Susa had long been in contact with.
entries.note: Susa administrative and legal tablet corpus, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Inshushinak, god of Susa, and the religion of a Bronze Age kingdom

entries.label: Inshushinak, God of Susa
entries.hint: Puzur-Inshushinak's own name — 'servant of Inshushinak' — reflects the central place of Susa's patron deity in Elamite royal ideology from this early period onward; Inshushinak would remain the presiding god of Susa and a figure in Elamite royal titulature for the next fifteen centuries.

entries.label: Royal Dedications at the Susa Temples
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-era rulers recorded temple construction and dedication in their own royal inscriptions, continuing a pattern of kings legitimating their rule partly through visible religious patronage — the same basic logic of temple-building kingship attested across contemporary Mesopotamia, expressed in Elam's own religious idiom.
